items.content:
I’ve left Anthropic after more than a year of working on Claude Code and seeing it scale larger than I ever imagined.

I have really loved working at Ant and believe deeply in the mission, and most of all, the idea of a race to the top.

The idea that if we work hard and responsibly, we can raise the bar and inspire others to great outcomes. And if we all push each other to be better, things can be radically good. I will carry the spirit of this with me forever.

My colleagues at Anthropic are the most talented, thoughtful, competent, and earnest people I have ever met. I am glad they are at the wheel and trust them deeply.

To the community on X, thank you for everything. You’ve made this the most fun (and sometimes stressful) job I’ve ever had.

For me, it is time for a bit of a break before diving into something new.

If you want more excellent Claude Code content, you should follow @addyosmani , @lydiahallie, @_catwu, @ClaudeDevs  and of course @bcherny who started it all.

items.title: the negative case against AI gets stronger every day; even Altman admits the problems are very serio...
items.content:
the negative case against AI gets stronger every day; even Altman admits the problems are very serious with no obvious solution.

the positive case, meanwhile, looks weaker every day. a quote from Apollo’s Torsten Slok:

“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech. Revenue per worker is… flat for the S&P 493…. Profit margins are… flat for the S&P 493…. No signs of AI boosting [measured] productivity growth…. Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending… as a cost center…. Mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it. As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited.”

https://t.co/DIFgO2XiA2

items.content:
Google seriously surprises me. Or I don't understand anything about the web economy.

When everyone realized that the web was the new world economy, it became clear that controlling the browser meant controlling the entry point to this economy. 

Google responded by creating Chrome, the best and fastest browser at the time, which supported extensions, giving it a virtually infinite set of features. 

Since then, Google has managed to stay ahead of the competition, preventing any rival from building a sufficiently better browser and ecosystem to convince users to switch.

Now everyone realizes that whoever controls the agentic harness controls the new agentic web, which, as we all see, is replacing the human web, where the browser rules.

Unless Google has a plan to transform Chrome into an agentic harness, I don't see how they will manage to keep their position as the entry point to the web.

2. In the real world, intelligence is not everythin A virus is "a million times stupider than you" but can still kill you. So can a cone shell, or a tiger.

items.content:
The Concise TypeScript Book by Simone Poggiali (2023) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks.

TypeScript is a free, open-source programming language developed by Microsoft that builds on top of JavaScript by adding static typing. It is considered a "superset" of JavaScript, meaning that any valid JavaScript code is also valid TypeScript code. 

Because web browsers and servers cannot run TypeScript directly, a compiler transpiles (converts) the code back into clean, standard JavaScript before it is deployed. Essentially, TypeScript acts as a strict development-time safety net to make writing complex applications smoother.

The textbook presents a practical, concise guide to TypeScript’s type system, compiler behavior, setup, and modern JavaScript support, helping developers write safer code and use TypeScript effectively in real projects.
